body:
The original intent of the spec was to give user-agents (who have much, much more information about a given users' context and preferences than authors ever can) the freedom to innovate on their actual selection mechanics over time. Authors provide the information UAs can't know in srcset and sizes, and then UAs own the selection decision, which they (hopefully) make intelligently, based (possibly) on information authors can't know.

Chrome did once  select smaller resources when users were in a "data-saver" mode. And Chrome also re-uses cached resources, if they're large enough (even if they overshoot the density target). Those are the only two instances I know of of a browser actually using the freedom the spec gives them, but both of them are (or, in the case of data-saver mode, were) hugely significant.

If we do give authors (who know the most about the importance of the *content*) more influence here, I want the tools they get to be coarse, because UAs do have more information about users' contexts and *could* do a better job than authors at setting an actual resolution target (even if they currently often don't). Instead of a multiplier that would require the actual selection mechanics to be specified and set in stone (and forbid UAs from making user-focused decisions based on the extra info they have), maybe we could give authors something like `fetchpriority`, but for resolution? `resolutionpriority`?
@austinh How is AirBnB actually lying, now? Do you bake the equivalent of a multiplier into your sizes? If so, what is that multiplier set at, in which contexts?

We actually lie about the width descriptors instead of sizes - our solution is even more nuanced than the examples given above. We inflate or deflate them based on various metrics we care about. It is indeed a multiplier. It achieves the same result but is technically not spec compliant. However we do so because it works with auto sizing as well as eager sizing and provides us the lever we want that the browser does not. 

Another open source example that attempts a similar strategy.
https://github.com/aFarkas/lazysizes/tree/gh-pages/plugins/optimumx




Say we have img.jpeg?w=720 800w this means we can serve a 720 image as if it was an 800w image. We only have so many image variants, but we have fluid grids/containers, and sometimes we want to be able to influence the variant selected at different times. We also have the concept of a density floor and ceiling. This "lying" width descriptor lets us put that all into a math equation that we can tweak. For us, at scale, we've found the balance between quality and performance to be more nuanced and results in significant revenue differences.


Some more examples: 
Hero images we may want boosted quality, especially if we know we will perform an animation with a larger image. So we prevent downloading two separate images and just load a larger one up front, even if its oversized for the initial container. 

3x devices we may want to cap at 2.5 density because its imperceptible.

We also have the concept of low data mode - and we fetch one ladder lower on our images (720 instead of 960 for example). I know chrome does something similar but webkit/firefox doesnt.

We can do all of this on native quite easily because we control the image fetching pipeline, caching layer etc, on ios/android etc. but the web limits our ability to express these intents. So cross platform parity is another motivator for us.

Basically, we experiment with these values heavily, and right now the browser doesnt give us the ability to do this according to the spec. We can do it with a hack, but would prefer not to.


We think the browsers can continue to clamp or set limits on their own, but we would like a way to influence this with developer intent. Sometimes the browsers don’t know our product the way we do. We would like more power over that choice of image.

@eeeps "the browsers would optimize it later" was well intentioned - but in practice, what happened is that interop won, and, to the best of my knowledge/research, no browser ever shipped an implementation-defined nuance for this in the ~11 years that responsive images exist.

I think we should change the mindset, and be clear about which source should be chosen, perhaps allowing UAs more specific leniancies:
- The UA MAY clamp the resolution further
- The UA MAY choose to keep an existing image and not choose a new one to avoid additional fetches

In addition we should give authors a bit more control over the knobs, given that the origins themselves measure their performance in context and can account for how they tweak the knobs in their business metrics.

The current escape hatch the spec gives authors if they want to control selection is `<picture>`, but if all you want is to control the resolution target in UAs' current defacto `srcset` selection algorithm, calculating all those `media` queries is quite unwieldy (though theoretically possible).

The argument about UAs' main incentive being interop vs authors' being business metrics, which provide tighter feedback loops and are more aligned with better outcomes for users, is a strong one.

I'm sad browsers didn't do *more* user-contextual adaptation (or even universal density-capping), but I don't want to limit them to the little bit of it that Chrome actually did do, forever. If we defined a more-explicit algorithm with more input from authors, but at the end said, "UAs MAY select a different resource based on user context and preferences" or whatever – do we think UAs could use that in the future? Or is the interop barrier too strong?

Lastly, I worry about complexity. [Many authors already struggle with responsive images](https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/media#fig-29). I don't want to hold sophisticated authors like AirBnB back, but I also don't want to make responsive images and the mental model we're asking authors to build up around them more complicated than they already are.

>     I'm sad browsers didn't do _more_ user-contextual adaptation (or even universal density-capping), but I don't want to limit them to the little bit of it that Chrome actually did do, forever. If we defined a more-explicit algorithm with more input from authors, but at the end said, "UAs MAY select a different resource based on user context and preferences" or whatever – do we think UAs could use that in the future? Or is the interop barrier too strong?

Perhaps it's better to keep the reality in the spec, and add the implementation-defined escape hatch if and when a UA actually wants to do that?

Otherwise, what would happen in practice with this kind of MAY is that advanced users and frameworks would rely on the de-facto implementation and would game them to act as if they had the right knobs (evidence: that's the current reality), and that would enshrine those de-facto decisions into an unspecified webcompat issue. So it's better to specify them based on what implementations do now, and when we know better, do better.

>     Lastly, I worry about complexity. [Many authors already struggle with responsive images](https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/media#fig-29). I don't want to hold sophisticated users like AirBnB back, but I also don't want to make responsive images and the mental model we're asking devs to build up around them more complicated than they already are.

True, but also this is purely elective no? Authors who don't use it wouldn't/shouldn't suffer from the complexity.

Something like densitytarget="2.0" could work. 

Its a density target that the browser aims for (default: 1.0, as today) and is completely
Opt-in. I agree on the point of complexity, most websites will just use a simple img tag and maybe a srcset - and could still do that. But advanced users should be empowered too. 

We did try to use media queries @eeeps  but we found it to be unwieldy and added significant complexity to our source set generation code. It also wasnt ideal with auto sizes. 


Then we stumbed upon lying to the browser about the width descriptor in a srcset and realized it simplified our code down to simple multiplication, at the expense of going against the spec and relying entirely on the implementation today. We know that one day our images could break if somehow the browsers changed their implementation. Hopefully that provides more evidence for somehow formalizing some way to do what we are trying to do in the spec.
Opened https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/13077 to discuss the "implementation defined" issue more in general.

For our purposes we found no reason to provide candidates for higher densities than 2x.
We find it unfortunate that a device that does have a higher density will use more bandwidth that we would have liked to render our pages.

Being able to set a cap, "this page assumes a max of 2x" would make it possible to reduce this bandwidth and power consumption.
